crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: Syndromic Surveillance
children.blurb: Syndromic surveillance is the near-real-time collection and analysis of health-related data that precede or substitute for confirmed diagnoses, such as emergency department chief complaints, over-the-counter medication sales, school absenteeism, and call center triage notes.

children.name: Outbreak Mapping
children.blurb: Outbreak mapping uses AI to detect, visualize, and forecast disease spread across populations.

children.name: Vaccine Waning Models
children.blurb: Vaccine waning models estimate how protection from vaccination declines over time, using observed infection, hospitalization, or antibody data.

children.name: Social Determinants of Health
children.blurb: Social determinants of health (SDOH) refer to the conditions in which people are born, grow, live, work, and age, including housing, income, education, employment, food access, transportation, and social support.

children.name: Allocating Scarce Resources
children.blurb: Allocating scarce resources in epidemiology and population health covers the use of AI to decide who gets a limited good or service when demand exceeds supply.

sections.body: Epidemiology and population health is the study of how disease and health conditions spread and persist across groups, not just individuals. AI in this field is used to scan routine data streams for early signs of outbreaks, to combine case counts with mobility and environmental data for mapping, to estimate how immunity fades after vaccination, to model how housing, income, and access to care shape outcomes, and to support decisions about who receives limited treatments or vaccines. These are operational systems in some public health agencies, though many remain pilot projects or research prototypes. The work often runs on messy, delayed, and incomplete data, which is the normal condition of population health rather than an exception. This site tracks 1000 medical AI models, and the pages in this section describe how a portion of that work is applied at the level of communities and populations.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: Some parts are relatively mature. Syndromic surveillance systems that flag unusual patterns in emergency department visits or over the counter drug sales are widely used, and outbreak mapping has become faster with genomic and mobility data. Vaccine waning models are useful for understanding average trends but struggle with new variants, uneven prior exposure, and incomplete reporting. Social determinants models can reveal strong associations, yet they often confuse correlation with cause and can encode historical inequities in the data. Allocation models can make trade offs explicit, but they cannot settle the ethical questions about whose life or wellbeing should be prioritized. The honest limits are data quality, timeliness, transparency, and the gap between a prediction and a public health action.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages here form a chain from detection to response. Syndromic Surveillance is the front door, covering how routine health data are scanned for early signals that something is changing. Outbreak Mapping takes those signals and asks where cases are, how they move, and what spatial patterns reveal. Vaccine Waning Models sit alongside them by estimating how protection declines over time and what that means for population immunity. Social Determinants of Health widens the frame to the living and working conditions that shape who gets sick and who recovers. Allocating Scarce Resources is the downstream page, describing how models and frameworks are used when demand for care, vaccines, or treatments exceeds supply, and a reader would go to each for a different layer of the same problem, from signal to map to immunity to social context to hard choices.
